data: Surface temperatures swing 610°C in a single day. No atmosphere — just raw exposure to space.
The smallest planet. Its highly elliptical orbit (e=0.206) makes it accelerate noticeably near perihelion. Despite being closest to the Sun, Venus is hotter.
Mariner 10 — NASA, 1974–75 (first spacecraft to visit Mercury; three flybys mapped ≈ 45 % of the surface)
MESSENGER — NASA, 2011–15 (first orbiter; complete surface map, gravity field, magnetic field, ice in polar craters)
BepiColombo — ESA / JAXA, 2018 launch · Mercury orbit insertion late 2026 (dual orbiter: MPO + Mio)
Mercury's 0.206 eccentricity is the highest of the 8 planets — at perihelion the Sun appears 1.5× larger in its sky than at aphelion.
The perihelion-aphelion swing (46–70 million km) drives huge differences in solar flux — Mercury's surface heats and cools more than any other planet.
Vis-viva is what shows Mercury speeding up dramatically at perihelion and slowing at aphelion — a 12 km/s swing.
Mercury's axial tilt is essentially zero (0.034°), so the bottoms of polar craters never see sunlight — and water ice survives there despite the planet's heat.
Three missions span Mercury's exploration: Mariner 10 (1974), MESSENGER (2011–15), and BepiColombo (orbit insertion late 2026).
How stretched the orbit is — zero is a perfect circle, one is a parabolic escape.
The two extreme points on every elliptical orbit: closest approach, and farthest.
How fast a body is moving at any point on its orbit — given just its current radius and the orbit's semi-major axis.
Why Earth has seasons, why Uranus rolled onto its side, and why Venus spins backward.
What's at each planet right now: from MRO at Mars to Juno at Jupiter — while Venus has had no orbiter since Akatsuki ended in 2025.
